# Homology and multiple sequence alignments {#msa}

Homologous genes share a common ancestor. When we line up homologous sequences in a **multiple sequence alignment (MSA)**, we can see which positions changed over evolution and which stayed the same, and that tells us what parts of a protein matter.

In this lab you will follow the workflow real researchers use:

**get sequences → align them → build a tree → find where the protein changes (and where it doesn't)**


## Part A: MSH mutations

Our protein is **MSH2**, a DNA mismatch repair protein. In humans, damage to MSH2 causes Lynch syndrome, a hereditary cancer predisposition. By the end you will be able to answer: *which parts of this protein are the most important, and how can we tell?*

***

### A1. Load the tools

The packages are already installed on the cluster. In RStudio, create a new R Markdown file called `Lab_5.Rmd` in your `BIOL123/Lab_5` folder, and load them:

```r

library(ggmsa)        # drawing alignments
library(phangorn)     # building trees
library(dplyr)        # data wrangling
library(ggplot2)      # plotting
library(tibble)       # tables
```

### A2. Get the sequences

We will download manually reviewed MSH2 proteins from UniProt (a curated protein database) directly into R:

```r
url <- "https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/stream?format=fasta&query=%28gene%3AMSH2%29+AND+%28reviewed%3Atrue%29"
download.file(url, "msh2_all.fasta")

seqs <- readAAStringSet("msh2_all.fasta")

# UniProt names are long, so keep only the short ID (like MSH2_HUMAN)
names(seqs) <- sub("^sp\\|[^|]+\\|([^ ]+) .*", "\\1", names(seqs))
seqs
```

To keep things manageable, we will use the human sequence plus 14 others:

```r
 # Lets save the sequences in a file for us to use them in different programs
writeXStringSet(seqs, "msh2_subset.fasta")
```

```{block, type='rmdwarning'}
**G-INS-i**: `mafft --globalpair --maxiterate 1000 msh2_subset.fasta > aln_gins.fasta`
**L-INS-i** `mafft --localpair  --maxiterate 1000 msh2_subset.fasta > aln_linsi.fasta`
```

### A4. Build a tree from the alignment

An alignment tells us which positions are homologous, so we can measure how different each pair of sequences is and build a tree of their relationships. We will use the **neighbor-joining** method, with bootstrapping to measure how much we can trust each branch.

```r
pd   <- phyDat(as.matrix(aln), type = "AA")
dm   <- dist.ml(pd, model = "WAG")     # pairwise distances between sequences
tree <- midpoint(NJ(dm))               # build the tree and root it at its midpoint

# Bootstrap: repeat the tree-building 100 times on resampled columns
bs <- bootstrap.phyDat(pd, function(x) NJ(dist.ml(x, model = "WAG")), bs = 100)

plotBS(tree, bs, p = 50, type = "phylogram", cex = 0.8)

support <- prop.clades(tree, bs)   # how many of the 100 bootstrap trees contain each branch

plot(tree, type = "phylogram", cex = 0.9)
nodelabels(ifelse(support >= 50, support, ""), frame = "none",adj = c(1.1, -0.4), cex = 0.8, col = "firebrick")
```

The numbers on the branches are bootstrap values (out of 100). Higher means more support.

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 8 - 9
- Include your tree. Do the animals group together? The fungi? Does it look like the species tree you expect?
- Find a branch with low bootstrap support (below 70). What does low support mean? What would you try to improve it?
```

**Does the alignment matter?** Re-run the three code chunks above using `aln <- aln_auto` and then `aln <- aln_gins`.

### A5. Where are the most (and fewest) changes?

Now for the question that matters biologically: **which parts of MSH2 stay the same across species (probably important) and which change a lot (probably tolerate change)?**

#### Step 1: Measure conservation at every position

For each column in the alignment, we calculate the fraction of sequences that share the most common amino acid. 1 means everyone is identical, and lower numbers mean more variation.

```r
m <- as.matrix(aln)

conservation <- apply(m, 2, function(x) {
  x <- x[x != "-"]                     # ignore gaps
  if (length(x) == 0) return(NA)
  max(table(x)) / length(x)
})
```

#### Step 2: Use human residue numbers

Alignment columns do not match the real protein positions because of gaps. We want everything numbered by the **human MSH2 protein**, so we count residues along the human row:

```r
human <- m[grep("MSH2_HUMAN", rownames(m)), ]

cons <- tibble(
  column       = seq_along(human),
  residue      = ifelse(human == "-", NA, cumsum(human != "-")),
  conservation = conservation
) |>
  filter(!is.na(residue))

# A smoothed line (average of 15 neighboring residues) is easier to read
cons$smooth <- as.numeric(stats::filter(cons$conservation, rep(1/15, 15), sides = 2))

head(cons)
```

#### Step 3: Find the protein's domains

Domains are parts of a protein with a specific job. Real researchers get them from databases.

1. Go to [InterPro](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/)  and search for **P43246** (human MSH2) in Search by Text.
2. Open the **Family & Domains** section. Also look at for P43246.
3. Fill in the table below with at least **three** domains or regions, using their start and end positions.

```r
domains <- tibble(
  domain = c("Domain 1", "Domain 2", "Domain 3","Domain 4"),   # replace with the real names
  start  = c(1, 125, 300, 620),                           # replace with the real start positions
  end    = c(124, 297, 507, 934)                            # replace with the real end positions
)
domains
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Question 11
- Paste your `domains` table. What does each domain do?
```

#### Step 4: Plot conservation along the protein with the domains

```r
ggplot(cons, aes(residue, conservation)) +
  geom_rect(data = domains,
            aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = 0, ymax = 1, fill = domain),
            alpha = 0.25, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(y = smooth), linewidth = 0.9, colour = "firebrick", na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Position in human MSH2 (amino acid number)",
       y = "Conservation (1 = identical in all species)",
       fill = "Domain") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("msh2_conservation_domains.png", width = 12, height = 4, dpi = 200)
```

And a number for each domain:

```r
domains |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(mean_conservation = mean(cons$conservation[cons$residue >= start & cons$residue <= end],
                                  na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
- Are there stretches between domains that are much less conserved? What might that tell you about those regions?
```

### A6. Real-world connection: mutations that cause disease

If a position is the same across all species, a change there is more likely to harm the protein. Researchers use this idea to judge whether a human mutation might cause disease.

1. Go to [ClinVar](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/) and search `MSH2[gene]`. Filter for **missense** variants (single amino acid changes).
2. Choose **three pathogenic** variants and **three benign** variants. Note the position in each (for example, `p.Gly67Arg` is position 67).
3. Add them to the code below and plot them on your conservation figure:

```r
variants <- tibble(
  position = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA),       # replace with your six positions
  type     = c("Pathogenic", "Pathogenic", "Pathogenic",
               "Benign", "Benign", "Benign")
)

variants <- variants |>
  left_join(cons, by = c("position" = "residue"))

variants
```

```r
ggplot(cons, aes(residue, conservation)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = variants, aes(position, conservation, colour = type), size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Pathogenic = "firebrick", Benign = "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "Position in human MSH2", y = "Conservation", colour = "ClinVar") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 15 - 16
- Include your table and plot. Are the pathogenic variants at more conserved positions than the benign ones?
- Would you trust conservation alone to decide whether a mutation is harmful? What other evidence would you want?
```


## Part B: DNA detective: solving a case with multiple sequence alignments

A **multiple sequence alignment (MSA)** lines up several DNA or protein sequences so that every column is the *same position* in every sequence. Once they are lined up, any difference you see is a **mutation**, and you can count them, draw a family tree from them, and ask whether they matter.

That one idea is behind a lot of real-world work:

- matching DNA from a crime scene to a suspect
- tracking which variant of a virus is spreading
- understanding how a single DNA change can cause a disease

In Part B you will do the first and the last: **B1** is a fictional case and **B2** uses real data from a real disease. Both use exactly the same steps: *get sequences, align, compare.*

***

### B1. The case of the missing cheesecake

```{block, type='rmdnote'}
This case and all of its DNA sequences are **made up** for teaching. Any resemblance to a real person is a coincidence.
```

**The story.** Liam left a birthday cheesecake in the lab fridge. This morning it was gone, and the only clue was a fork in the sink. The lab swabbed the fork and sequenced a short piece of **mitochondrial DNA** (160 bases). Mitochondrial DNA is handy for detective work because it is inherited from your mother and it is present in many copies per cell, so it can be read even from tiny samples.

The lab also took a cheek swab from six suspects and sequenced the same 160-base region.

| Name | Why they were suspicious |
|---|---|
| Sophia | Is generally suspicious |
| Hannah | Was "working late" |
| Fae | "Just wanted a small slice" |
| Professor | Claims to be on a diet |
| Ghaniel | Brought the cheesecake |
| Elliott | Was seen in the hallway fighting cockroaches |

Your job: **use an alignment to figure out whose DNA is on the fork.**

#### Step 1: Get the sequences

In your `Lab_5.Rmd`, load the packages (some are already loaded from Part A, which is fine):

```r
library(Biostrings)   # reading sequences
library(ggmsa)        # drawing alignments
library(ape)          # trees
library(phangorn)     # building the tree
library(ggplot2)
```

Download the case file and look at it:

```r
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Tabima/BIOL123/master/Lab_5/crime_scene.fasta",
              "crime_scene.fasta")

dna <- readDNAStringSet("crime_scene.fasta")
dna
width(dna)
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 17 - 18
- How many sequences are in the file? Which one is the evidence?
- Do all the sequences have the same length? Which one is different? Why can't we just compare the sequences letter by letter?
```

#### Step 2: Align the sequences

run MAFFT:

```r
system("mafft --auto crime_scene.fasta > crime_aln.fasta")
```

You will see some messages scroll by while MAFFT works. That is normal.

#### Step 3: Look at the alignment

Back in R, load the alignment and draw it wrapped into blocks of 60 columns:

```r
aln <- readDNAStringSet("crime_aln.fasta")

ggmsa(aln, start = 1, end = width(aln)[1], color = "Chemistry_NT",
      seq_name = TRUE, char_width = 0.5, ref = "Evidence_CoffeeCup") +
  facet_msa(field = 60)
```

Each row is one person, and each column is one position in the DNA. Letters that differ from the others stand out in a different color. Dashes (`-`) are **gaps** where the aligner added a blank because one sequence is missing a base.

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 19 - 20
- Include your figure. Find the gap. Which sequence has it?
- Looking only at the picture, which suspect(s) do you think match the evidence best? Which do you think are clearly different?
```

#### Step 4: Count the differences

Eyeballing is not evidence. Let's count how many positions differ between every pair of sequences (a gap counts as one difference):

```r
m <- as.matrix(aln)

diffs <- sapply(rownames(m), function(a)
           sapply(rownames(m), function(b) sum(m[a, ] != m[b, ])))
diffs
```

To see just the comparison against the evidence:

```r
sort(diffs["Evidence_CoffeeCup", ])
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 21 - 22
- Paste the sorted result. How many differences does each suspect have compared to the evidence?
- Who is the best match? Is there anyone you would **not** rule out yet? Explain your reasoning.
```

#### Step 5: Draw the family tree

A tree shows who is most closely related. Sequences with few differences end up close together:

```r
tree <- midpoint(NJ(as.dist(diffs)))          # build the tree and put the root in the middle
tree$edge.length <- pmax(tree$edge.length, 0)  # tiny negative branch lengths can appear; set them to 0

plot(tree, type = "phylogram", cex = 1.2, edge.width = 2, label.offset = 0.3,
     x.lim = c(0, max(node.depth.edgelength(tree)) * 1.6),
     tip.color = ifelse(grepl("Evidence", tree$tip.label), "red", "black"))
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 23 - 24
- Include your tree. Who sits closest to the evidence? Do the suspects split into groups?
- Two suspects are very close to each other on the tree. Why might the DNA of two different people be nearly identical? (Hint: where does mitochondrial DNA come from?)
```

### B2. The same tools on a real disease

In B1 you looked for tiny differences between people. Now we use the same steps to see **how one tiny change in DNA can cause a disease.**

**Sickle cell disease** is caused by a change in the gene for **beta-globin (HBB)**, one of the proteins that makes up hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in your blood. People with the disease have a single amino acid swapped in this protein.

#### Step 1: Get the normal protein

```r
download.file("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P68871.fasta", "hbb_human.fasta")

normal <- readAAStringSet("hbb_human.fasta")
names(normal) <- "Normal"
normal
width(normal)
```

#### Step 2: Make the sickle cell version

The sickle cell change replaces the glutamate (E) at position 7 of the protein with a valine (V). First, check that position 7 really is a glutamate in the normal protein:

```r
chars <- strsplit(as.character(normal), "")[[1]]
chars[7]
```

Now make the mutated copy and save both:

```r
chars[7] <- "V"
sickle <- AAString(paste(chars, collapse = ""))

pair <- AAStringSet(c(Normal = as.character(normal),
                      Sickle = as.character(sickle)))
writeXStringSet(pair, "hbb_pair.fasta")
```

```{block, type='rmdnote'}
**A numbering quirk:** textbooks call this mutation "E6V" (glutamate to valine at position 6), but our database counts the starting methionine as position 1, so we call it position 7. It is the same mutation.
```

#### Step 3: Align and find the change

```r
system("mafft --auto hbb_pair.fasta > hbb_pair_aln.fasta")

pair_aln <- readAAStringSet("hbb_pair_aln.fasta")

ggmsa(pair_aln, start = 1, color = "Chemistry_AA", seq_name = TRUE, char_width = 0.6) +
  facet_msa(field = 60)
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 27 - 29
- Include your figure. How many differences are there between the normal and the sickle sequences? In which column?
- Look up glutamate (E) and valine (V). One is charged and loves water; the other repels water. How are they different?
- Hemoglobin works in a watery environment inside red blood cells. In sickle cell disease the molecules stick to each other and form long fibers. How could swapping E for V on the surface of a protein cause that?
```

#### Step 4: Is this position important in other animals?

If evolution kept this position the same across many species, a change there is more likely to cause trouble. Let's check by downloading beta-globin from six animals:

```r
get_beta <- function(taxid) {
  q   <- sprintf('(protein_name:"Hemoglobin subunit beta") AND (organism_id:%s) AND (reviewed:true)', taxid)
  url <- paste0("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/search?format=fasta&size=1&query=",
                URLencode(q, reserved = TRUE))
  f <- tempfile()
  download.file(url, f, quiet = TRUE)
  readAAStringSet(f)
}

taxa   <- c(human = 9606, mouse = 10090, cow = 9913, horse = 9796, chicken = 9031, zebrafish = 7955)
betas <- do.call(c, unname(lapply(taxa, get_beta)))
names(betas) <- sub("^sp\\|[^|]+\\|([^ ]+) .*", "\\1", names(betas))

class(betas)
writeXStringSet(betas, "beta_species.fasta")
```

Align them using `MAFFT`

```r
system('mafft --auto beta_species.fasta > beta_species_aln.fasta')
```

Then in R, look at the start of the alignment and find the column that matches human position 7:

```r
aln2 <- readAAStringSet("beta_species_aln.fasta")
library(patchwork)

w      <- 60
len    <- width(aln2)[1]
starts <- seq(1, len, by = w)

blocks <- lapply(starts, function(s)
  ggmsa(aln2, start = s, end = min(s + w - 1, len),
        color = "Chemistry_AA", seq_name = TRUE, char_width = 0.5) +
    geom_seqlogo())

wrap_plots(blocks, ncol = 1)

m2    <- as.matrix(aln2)
human <- m2[grep("HUMAN", rownames(m2)), ]
col7  <- which(human != "-")[7]       # the alignment column of human residue 7

m2[, col7]                            # what each species has at that spot
table(m2[, col7])
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 30 - 31
- What amino acids do the different animals have at this position? Is it the same in all of them, or does it vary?
- Based on what you see, would you expect a change at this position to be tolerated or harmful? What other evidence would you want before deciding?
```
